a: Absurdism and nihilism are two distinct philosophical schools that both emerged from existentialist thought but draw very different conclusions. Nihilism (from Latin nihil, meaning nothing) is the belief that life has no intrinsic meaning, purpose, or value. Friedrich Nietzsche famously declared 'God is dead' and warned that nihilism would be the crisis of the modern age. Nihilists argue that moral values are baseless, knowledge is impossible, and existence is meaningless. Absurdism, primarily associated with Albert Camus (The Myth of Sisyphus, 1942), agrees that life has no inherent meaning but rejects the nihilistic conclusion that this leads to despair. Instead, Camus argues we should embrace the absurd — the conflict between humanity's desire for meaning and the universe's indifference — and live with passion and rebellion despite it. The key difference: nihilism says 'life is meaningless, so nothing matters,' while absurdism says 'life is meaningless, so we are free to create our own meaning and joy.' Unlike nihilism which often leads to passivity or despair, absurdism encourages active engagement with life. Sisyphus, condemned to endlessly push a boulder up a hill only to watch it roll down, is Camus's absurd hero — he finds meaning in the struggle itself. Camus's famous conclusion: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.'
